paragraphs.title: Failed Reliance on Egypt and Rejection of God’s Word

easy.explanation: The passage addresses God’s people who made plans without consulting him.
They went down into Egypt and trusted in Pharaoh’s strength.
easy.q: Where did the people go for help?

easy.explanation: The KJV says they “have not asked at my mouth.”
easy.q: What had they not done before making their plans?

medium.explanation: They sought strength from Pharaoh and trusted in the shadow of Egypt.
medium.q: Why did the people turn to Egypt?

medium.explanation: The strength and shadow of Egypt would become their shame and confusion.
medium.q: What would reliance on Egypt bring to Judah?

medium.explanation: The verse describes riches and treasures being carried by donkeys and camels.
medium.q: In the phrase “The burden of the beasts of the south,” what does “burden” mean?

answers: It shows the costly and perilous journey toward help that cannot profit them
It proves Egypt was stronger than God
It presents the wilderness as a place of celebration
challenge.explanation: The lions, serpents, trouble, and anguish underline the danger and uselessness of the journey.
challenge.q: How does the dangerous journey through the wilderness emphasize the failure of relying on Egypt?

answers: Their help would be vain and accomplish nothing
challenge.explanation: The passage says, “the Egyptians shall help in vain, and to no purpose.”
challenge.q: Why are the Egyptians described as unable to profit Judah?

answers: Human plans without God versus help that truly profits
challenge.explanation: Judah planned without God and trusted Egypt, but Egypt could not provide genuine help.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verses 1–7?

paragraphs.title: Rejection of Prophecy and the Consequences of False Security

answers: The warning on a table and in a book
easy.explanation: The message was to be written as a witness for the future.
easy.q: What did the Lord command Isaiah to write?

easy.explanation: They wanted pleasant words and false prophecies instead of the truth.
easy.q: What did the people ask the seers and prophets to do?

easy.explanation: The Lord said, “In quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.”
easy.q: Where would their strength have been found?

medium.explanation: They despised God’s word and relied on oppression and crookedness.
medium.q: What caused the coming collapse described as a broken wall?

medium.explanation: The Lord says, “and ye would not,” showing their refusal.
medium.q: How did the people respond to salvation through returning and resting?

answers: Tell us pleasant words instead of hard rebuke
medium.explanation: The people preferred comfortable and deceptive messages over God’s correction.
medium.q: What does “speak unto us smooth things” mean?

answers: It would come slowly over many years
It would come suddenly after hidden weakness
challenge.explanation: The high wall appears strong, but its breaking comes “suddenly at an instant.”
challenge.q: What does the image of a wall breaking suddenly teach about the judgment?

answers: They preferred comfortable messages to divine rebuke
They wanted teaching only about agriculture
challenge.explanation: They told the prophets not to speak right things and requested pleasing words instead.
challenge.q: How is the people’s demand for smooth prophecies connected with rejecting God’s word?

answers: Returning, resting, quietness, and confidence in God
challenge.explanation: The Lord connects salvation and strength with returning, rest, quietness, and confidence.
challenge.q: What path to salvation is presented in the passage?

paragraphs.title: Comfort, Guidance, and Abundance in the Land

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem.”

answers: Give them a treaty with Egypt
easy.explanation: He would be gracious and answer when he heard their cry.
easy.q: What would the Lord do when he heard their cry?

easy.explanation: The moon would be as the sun, and the sun would be sevenfold brighter.
easy.q: What would happen to the light of the moon and sun?

answers: By hearing a word behind them
medium.explanation: They would hear, “This is the way, walk ye in it.”
medium.q: How would the people receive guidance on their way?

answers: Cast them away and reject them
medium.explanation: They would defile and cast away their silver and golden images.
medium.q: What would the people do with their graven images?

medium.explanation: The earth would produce abundant food and pasture.
medium.q: What does “fat and plenteous” mean in the description of the land?

answers: God’s guidance leads the people away from idols and back to his way
The guidance teaches them to make idols
challenge.explanation: Hearing God’s direction and casting away idols both show spiritual restoration.
challenge.q: How are divine guidance and the rejection of idols connected?

answers: Through rain, crops, pasture, water, and light
challenge.explanation: The passage presents agricultural abundance, streams, pasture, and increased light.
challenge.q: How does the abundance of the land express comfort?

answers: A time of restoration, blessing, and redemption
challenge.explanation: The Lord’s healing of his people is accompanied by extraordinary light and renewed abundance.
challenge.q: What does the connection between healing and increased light suggest?

paragraphs.title: God’s Manifestation and Judgment on Assyria

easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Behold, the name of the Lord cometh from far.”
easy.q: Who comes from far in terrifying power?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “through the voice of the Lord shall the Assyrian be beaten down.”
easy.q: Which nation would be beaten down by the Lord’s voice?

answers: With a song and gladness of heart
easy.explanation: They would have a song and gladness as they went to the mountain of the Lord.
easy.q: How would God’s people respond to the Lord’s mighty work?

answers: Fire, storm, rushing water, and hailstones
medium.explanation: The passage describes devouring fire, an overflowing stream, tempest, and hailstones.
medium.q: Which signs accompany the Lord’s manifestation?

answers: Israel’s joy in the Lord’s deliverance
medium.explanation: The song and gladness contrast with the Lord’s judgment on the enemy.
medium.q: What does the song express in this passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the Lord’s defeat of the Assyrian power.
medium.q: What does “beaten down” mean in the statement about the Assyrian?

answers: Terrifying judgment on Assyria alongside joy for God’s people
Famine in Judah alongside plenty in Egypt
Peace with Assyria alongside war in Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The Lord’s coming brings fear and defeat to the enemy but song and gladness to his people.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verses 27–33?

answers: They emphasize his overwhelming power and the enemy’s inability to resist
They prove that Jerusalem must be abandoned
They describe only a harvest festival
challenge.explanation: The powerful natural images portray the force of divine judgment.
challenge.q: How do the fire and storm imagery express God’s judgment?

answers: It is a place prepared for the king as part of Assyria’s judgment
It is a resting place for Israel
It is a grain storehouse in Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: Tophet is described as a deep place of fire prepared for the king.
challenge.q: What is the significance of Tophet at the end of the passage?
